Hester Howard died about thirty hours after her son, on June 12, 1936. Both were buried in the same Cross Plains plot. Howard was 30, his mother 66.

question: H.P. Lovecraft died on March 15, 1937 in Providence's Jane Brown Memorial Hospital of intestinal cancer that had spread beyond treatment. He had been keeping detailed medical notes in a diary because he was curious about his own symptoms. His estate at death amounted to roughly $25. Two young readers and correspondents — devastated by his death — founded a small Wisconsin press in 1939 specifically to keep his work in print. They published his first hardback collection that year, securing his legacy. Who were the two founders?
choices: Frank Belknap Long and Clark Ashton Smith
Lin Carter and L. Sprague de Camp
context: Arkham House's first publication was The Outsider and Others (1939) — 1,268 copies, edited by Derleth and Wandrei from Lovecraft's manuscripts in Lovecraft's widow Sonia's possession. The press is named for Lovecraft's fictional New England city. Without Derleth and Wandrei's salvage operation, Lovecraft might have remained pulp-obscure. Derleth himself wrote dozens of mythos pastiches afterward, often criticized for systematizing what Lovecraft had left ambiguous. Wandrei was a poet and stockbroker, less prolific.

question: John W. Campbell took over Astounding Stories in October 1937 and renamed it Astounding Science-Fiction in early 1938. Over the next decade, he published the debut or early stories of every major Golden Age writer except Bradbury. Campbell paid above-market rates for the era (1 cent per word, sometimes 2). He famously bought a 1939 short story from a Brooklyn College student who had written it under the pen name 'Don A. Stuart' — but the byline was actually Campbell's own pseudonym, used for a 1934 story he had pre-Campbell. The 1939 sale that broke the new writer's career was not the same as the pseudonym confusion. That Brooklyn College student was a teenager when he sold his first story to Campbell. Who was he?
context: Asimov's first Campbell sale was 'Trends' (Astounding, July 1939) — he was 19. The Don A. Stuart pen name was Campbell's, used for stories like 'Twilight' (1934) and 'Who Goes There?' (1938) — the rationale was to write quietly literary stories that contrasted with his loud pulp 'Campbell' style. Heinlein's first sale to Campbell was 'Life-Line' (Astounding, August 1939) — one month after Asimov's debut. Both became Campbell's two flagship writers.

question: Edgar Rice Burroughs founded his own publishing company in 1923 — frustrated with what he considered insufficient royalties from established publishers — and personally incorporated as a corporation under California law, becoming arguably the first author to do so. By the late 1930s, his California estate at Tarzana was both his home and his corporate headquarters. The town of Tarzana, California (annexed by Los Angeles in 1936) actually took its name from his estate. Burroughs died on March 19, 1950, having sold over 100 million copies in his lifetime. His company is still publishing him. What was the corporate name?
context: Burroughs incorporated as a corporation on March 17, 1923. He had been writing for All-Story / Argosy under the pen name 'Normal Bean' (his Tarzan debut byline) since 1911. His Tarzana estate covered 540 acres of the San Fernando Valley; the town of Tarzana now houses 36,000 people. Edgar Rice Burroughs, Inc. is still owned by the family and licenses both Tarzan and the Mars/John Carter franchises. The 2012 Disney film John Carter was a major flop but is now a cult film.

question: Tolkien served in the Lancashire Fusiliers as a signals officer in 1916. He was sent to France in early June. By July 1 he was on the Somme front. He fought at Thiepval and Beaumont-Hamel. He contracted trench fever (a louse-borne illness, not as deadly as typhus or flu but debilitating) in late October and was invalided back to England on November 8, 1916. Of his four-member Oxford school club — the T.C.B.S. (Tea Club and Barrovian Society) — three were killed during the war. Two of them died in 1916 during the Somme campaign Tolkien himself fought in. What were those two T.C.B.S. friends' names?
answer: Rob Gilson and Geoffrey Bache Smith
choices: Rob Gilson and Geoffrey Bache Smith
Hugh Cary Gilson and Edward Williams
context: Rob Gilson was killed at La Boisselle on July 1, 1916 — the first day of the Somme. G.B. Smith died on December 3, 1916 of gangrene from a shell wound. The fourth T.C.B.S. member, Christopher Wiseman, survived the war. Tolkien edited Smith's poetry (A Spring Harvest, 1918) after his death. His Silmarillion mythology had been gestating since 1914; the war crystallized his sense of what fantasy was for. Charles Williams and Owen Barfield were later Inklings associates, not the T.C.B.S.

question: Frank Herbert worked for ten years on Dune before its 1965 hardcover publication by Chilton Books — a Philadelphia firm primarily known for publishing auto-repair manuals. The novel had been rejected by twenty publishers, including all the major science-fiction houses (Doubleday, Putnam, Ace, etc.). Herbert had originally researched Dune as a magazine article about Oregon's dunes and the U.S. Department of Agriculture's effort to use beach grass to stabilize them. He had a working title for the book that he eventually rejected as too on-the-nose. What was the working title?
context: The Spice Planet was a shorter early draft (1958) that Herbert later expanded into the full Dune novel; the original draft survived and was reconstructed by Brian Herbert and Kevin J. Anderson in 2005. Herbert's 1957 magazine article 'They Stopped the Moving Sands' was the project's seed. The Chilton hardcover went almost unnoticed at first; Ace Books's 1967 paperback made it a bestseller. Dune won both the Hugo (1966) and the inaugural Nebula (1966) — the first novel to win both.

question: Philip K. Dick wrote 44 novels between 1955 and his death in March 1982 — five months before Ridley Scott's Blade Runner premiered. Many of his last novels were drug-influenced and autobiographical. His 1981 novel about a divine encounter following a 1974 mystical episode was deeply influenced by what Dick called the 'Black Iron Prison' theory of reality. The novel takes its title from a four-letter acronym for the godlike intelligence. What was the 1981 novel called?
context: VALIS stands for Vast Active Living Intelligence System. The novel is the first of Dick's so-called VALIS Trilogy, with two 1982 companion books. VALIS is rooted in Dick's February-March 1974 experiences — what he called 2-3-74 — which he believed were either spiritual experiences, schizophrenic episodes, or signals from an alien-divine intelligence. He filled an 8,000-page Exegesis trying to understand them; a selection was published posthumously in 2011.

question: Tolkien wrote The Hobbit largely between 1930 and 1932 during his time as Rawlinson and Bosworth Professor of Anglo-Saxon at Oxford. The book famously opens with a line he scribbled on the back of an exam paper he was grading. He didn't know what a 'hobbit' was at the time — the word came first. The exam paper was for the School Certificate Examination in English. What was the opening line he scribbled?
answer: In a hole in the ground there lived a hobbit
choices: In a hole in the ground there lived a hobbit
Far over the misty mountains cold
There was once a hobbit who lived in a hole
Bilbo Baggins of Bag End was no ordinary hobbit
context: Tolkien said the line came to him 'out of nowhere' while he was looking at a blank examination booklet. He set it aside and only returned to writing the book around 1932. He read drafts aloud to his children. C.S. Lewis read it in manuscript around 1933 and pushed him to finish it. Susan Dagnall at George Allen & Unwin recommended publication. The first edition (September 21, 1937) had a print run of 1,500 copies.

question: Manly Wade Wellman was a 1930s pulp writer who became, in his second career, the leading practitioner of American folklore-horror fiction. From 1951 onward he wrote the John the Balladeer (or 'Silver John') stories — set in the Appalachian Mountains of North Carolina, featuring a wandering Korean War veteran with a silver-stringed guitar who confronts witches, devils, and dark fae rooted in actual Appalachian folklore. Wellman's silver-stringed-guitar conceit was rooted in real American folk-music tradition. He wrote his first Silver John story for which 1951 fantasy magazine?
answer: The Magazine of Fantasy and Science Fiction
choices: The Magazine of Fantasy and Science Fiction
Weird Tales after the Wright era end
Unknown Worlds, the Campbell sister title
Beyond Fantasy Fiction, the Galaxy spinoff
context: Wellman's 'O Ugly Bird!' appeared in F&SF in December 1951. The Silver John stories are characteristically narrated in first-person mountain dialect. Wellman won the British Fantasy Society's August Derleth Award (1975) for Worse Things Waiting; he also won the World Fantasy Lifetime Achievement Award in 1980. He died in 1986 in Chapel Hill, North Carolina at age 82. His Silver John novels include After Dark (1980) and The Lost and the Lurking (1981).

question: Karl Edward Wagner — a North Carolina physician-turned-writer and 1970s editor of the Year's Best Horror Stories anthology — created an immortal red-haired swordsman who is the literal Cain of Genesis, marked by God after killing his brother and condemned to wander Earth forever. Wagner's character debuted in a 1970 small-press novel and ran across roughly fifteen stories before Wagner's 1994 death. What was the character's name?
context: Kane's first novel Darkness Weaves was Wagner's 1970 debut with Powell Books. Wagner combined sword-and-sorcery with cosmic horror and biblical apocrypha. Kane is the original Cain, his red hair the mark God set upon him. The character is amoral and brilliant — Wagner explicitly rejected the heroic-fantasy mode of Howard or Tolkien. Kane novels include Bloodstone (1975), Dark Crusade (1976), and The Book of Kane (1985). Wagner died of alcoholism aged 48 in October 1994.

question: William Hope Hodgson wrote four major weird-fiction novels in the early 1900s before his death at Ypres in 1918 (he was 40, killed by a German artillery shell during the Battle of Mont Kemmel). His most cosmically ambitious novel, published 1912, is set far in the future on an Earth where the sun has gone dark and the last refuge of humanity is a colossal pyramid-fortress called the Last Redoubt, surrounded by monstrous creatures from beyond the lightless world. What was the novel called?
choices: The Boats of the Glen Carrig
context: The Night Land's prose imitates 17th-century English deliberately — Hodgson considered it formal scriptural style appropriate to the eschatological subject. The novel was reviewed unenthusiastically in 1912 but became a major influence on Lovecraft (who called it 'one of the most potent pieces of macabre imagination ever written'), Clark Ashton Smith, and later Gene Wolfe. Hodgson was a former merchant-marine officer; the sea-horror in his earlier novels The Boats of the Glen Carrig (1907) and The Ghost Pirates (1909) drew from his own North Atlantic experience.

question: Algernon Blackwood — the English fantasist and Society for Psychical Research investigator — published a 1907 novella widely considered one of the greatest weird stories ever written. Two friends canoeing down the Danube River in a wild section of central Europe (the borderland between Hungary and the Balkans) camp on a sandbar overgrown with thick willow trees. They begin to sense that the willows are watching them — and that something on the other side of the natural world is trying to break through. Lovecraft, in his 1927 essay on horror in literature, ranked it as the single finest piece of weird fiction he had ever read. What was the story called?
context: The Willows was published in The Listener and Other Stories (1907). Blackwood himself had canoed the Danube in 1900. His other major weird stories include The Wendigo (1910, the source of the modern North American Wendigo mythos in popular culture) and the John Silence stories — proto-psychic-investigator tales. Blackwood lived 1869-1951 and became a BBC radio personality in his later years, reading his own ghost stories on Christmas broadcasts.

question: M.R. (Montague Rhodes) James was a medieval scholar and Provost of Eton (later Cambridge's King's College) who wrote ghost stories to read aloud to friends at Christmas. He published four collections between 1904 and 1925. His stories defined what is now called the 'antiquarian ghost story' — bookish scholars, ancient artifacts, dusty cathedral libraries, slow-building dread. His 1911 collection includes a story about a Cambridge professor who pulls a strange bronze whistle out of a Roman ruin and finds something is now following him through the empty seaside hotel where he is staying. What was the story called?
answer: Oh, Whistle, and I'll Come to You, My Lad
choices: Oh, Whistle, and I'll Come to You, My Lad
The Treasure of Abbot Thomas (1904 tale)
Count Magnus and the Black Pilgrim Tale
context: Oh, Whistle was published in More Ghost Stories of an Antiquary (1911). The professor is named Parkins; the hotel is in the fictional Burnstow on the East Anglian coast. The story has been adapted twice by the BBC (1968 starring Michael Hordern, 2010 starring John Hurt). The whistle bears the Latin inscription 'Quis est iste qui venit' — 'Who is this who is coming?' James's collected stories were a major influence on H.P. Lovecraft and continue to be read aloud at Christmas in many English households.

question: On October 8, 1928 — three months before The Call of Cthulhu went to print — H.P. Lovecraft sat down to write a letter to Frank Belknap Long describing a story idea he had just had. The story would feature an Arkham professor whose vacation home in rural Vermont becomes the focus of a winged-crustacean alien race who mine for a metal called Tok'l. The aliens have a particular use for human brains, which they preserve in metal cylinders to carry their consciousness through interstellar travel. The story Lovecraft was incubating became, when published in Weird Tales in August 1930, his most overt science-fiction-horror hybrid. What was the story called?
choices: The Dreams in the Witch House
context: The aliens are the Mi-go (the Lovecraft-canon name for the Yuggoth Outer Ones), fungoid-crustacean entities that mine Vermont for rare minerals. They preserve a fugitive man's brain in a metal cylinder so it can converse from beyond the body. The story is set in the wake of the November 1927 Vermont floods, a real historical event. The 2011 H.P. Lovecraft Historical Society silent-film adaptation is considered the most accurate Lovecraft film made.

question: Tolkien's invented language for the Dwarves — Khuzdul — is a secret language the Dwarves rarely share with outsiders. Tolkien based its phonology on Semitic languages (Hebrew especially), in contrast to his Indo-European Elvish languages. Khuzdul has only a few surviving words in The Lord of the Rings, including the Dwarvish names for places and the war-cry the Dwarves use against the Balrog in the Mines of Moria during Gimli's outburst at Balin's tomb. What was that war-cry?
context: The cry translates as 'Axes of the Dwarves! The Dwarves are upon you!' Tolkien designed Khuzdul phonetically to feel angular and stone-like, matching the Dwarves' culture. The Dwarves' true names (in Khuzdul) are kept secret from outsiders; the names we know (Thorin, Balin, Gimli, etc.) are Mannish translations from a related Northern-Mannish tongue. Tolkien based the secret-language idea partly on Hebrew traditions about the Tetragrammaton.

question: Edgar Allan Poe published his first detective story — and arguably invented the genre — in Graham's Lady's and Gentleman's Magazine in April 1841. The narrator's friend, a brilliant impoverished aristocrat, solves the locked-room murder of two women whose injuries no human assailant could plausibly have inflicted. Conan Doyle would later acknowledge the story as the direct ancestor of Sherlock Holmes. The two murdered women were named in the story. What was their family name?
context: Madame and Mademoiselle L'Espanaye are murdered in The Murders in the Rue Morgue, the first Dupin story. The actual killer turns out to be an escaped orangutan from a Maltese sailor. Poe followed it with The Mystery of Marie Rogêt (1842) and The Purloined Letter (1844) — three Dupin stories total. Conan Doyle wrote in his autobiography Memories and Adventures (1924) that Sherlock Holmes was a direct descendant of Dupin, with Poe holding 'the master's place.'

question: Howard's bone-deep historical knowledge informed his lesser-known but possibly best work — his series about a Pictish king of post-Roman Britain who defies the imperial cohorts. The character was Howard's pre-Conan attempt at literary historical fantasy, and Howard wrote eight stories about him from 1926 to 1932. The Picts are a real ancient people of northern Britain; Howard's character is their dying king, fighting the encroaching Roman empire. What was the character's name?
context: Bran's signature story is 'Worms of the Earth' (Weird Tales, November 1932) — Bran descends into prehistoric darkness to call on a degenerate subterranean race to destroy a Roman governor. Howard's Bran stories appeared between 1926 and 1932. The Picts in Howard's mythos are the longest-running race; they survive into Conan's Hyborian Age as the savage forest-tribes of the West. Lovecraft praised 'Worms of the Earth' as Howard's finest single story.

question: Tolkien wrote thousands of letters about Middle-earth. His longest correspondence about his own published work was with Milton Waldman, an editor at Collins who briefly considered publishing The Silmarillion alongside LOTR in 1951. Tolkien's December 1951 letter to Waldman runs over 10,000 words and is the single best statement of the mythology's deeper themes. Tolkien identified one fall-from-grace pattern as the engine driving all of his Middle-earth tragedy — Fëanor, Sauron, Saruman, Boromir, and the Numenoreans all share it. What did Tolkien call this pattern in the letter?
answer: The desire of the lover for the Beloved Subcreated Thing made his own possession
choices: The desire of the lover for the Beloved Subcreated Thing made his own possession
The temptation by which industrial machinery destroys the bearer's soul
The biblical sin of pride straightforwardly imported from Genesis itself
The medieval doctrine of acedia translated into modern fantastic terms
context: Tolkien's Letter 131 to Waldman summarizes the entire legendarium. The fall begins with possessive love — wanting to own and control what one has made or what one loves, instead of letting it remain free. Fëanor's love for his Silmarils, Sauron's love for order, Saruman's love for knowledge — all become possessiveness. Tolkien rejected explicit allegory but favored 'applicability' (the reader's freedom to make connections). The full Waldman letter is reprinted as the preface to the 1977 Silmarillion edition.

question: Asimov's Three Laws of Robotics first appeared in formalized statement in his March 1942 Astounding story 'Runaround.' Asimov later credited a specific Astounding editor with codifying the laws into their final form during the editing process for several earlier robot stories. Who was the editor?
context: John W. Campbell edited Astounding Science Fiction from 1937 to 1971 and was a towering — if controversial — influence on the Golden Age of SF. Asimov's earliest robot stories ('Liar!' 1941, 'Robbie' 1940) hinted at the rules; Campbell pushed Asimov to formalize them. The Three Laws first appear in named form in 'Runaround' (March 1942 Astounding). Campbell also discovered and developed Robert Heinlein, A.E. van Vogt, Theodore Sturgeon, and Lester del Rey. Frederik Pohl edited Galaxy and If; Anthony Boucher edited F&SF; H.L. Gold founded Galaxy.

question: Edgar Allan Poe's 1841 story The Murders in the Rue Morgue introduced not only the world's first fictional detective but also the genre's bag of tools — the eccentric brilliant amateur, the slow-witted narrator-friend, the locked-room puzzle, the dramatic culminating reveal. Dupin solves the murders with a method Poe called what — a term that would eventually be borrowed for cryptography, criminology, and the cognitive sciences?
context: Poe used 'ratiocination' as a noun for systematic, reasoning analysis. He published three Dupin stories — Rue Morgue (1841), Marie Rogêt (1842), and The Purloined Letter (1844). Dupin's method blends induction from physical clues, deduction from behavior, and what we would now call profiling. Conan Doyle adopted nearly all of Poe's apparatus for Sherlock Holmes. Poe's term 'ratiocination' was the closest the 1840s came to articulating what twentieth-century cognitive science would call 'analytical reasoning.'

question: The Call of Cthulhu, published in the February 1928 issue of Weird Tales, contains a specific moment that Lovecraft scholars have identified as the literary birth of cosmic horror as a self-aware genre. In Part III of the story, the Norwegian sailor Gustaf Johansen's manuscript describes his crew of the schooner Emma making landfall on the strange island that has just emerged from the South Pacific. The island's geometry is non-Euclidean — angles that should be convex appear concave to the eye. A massive door in the cliff-face swings open inward and outward simultaneously. Cthulhu emerges. Johansen's specific physical description of the door's geometry was so striking it became a literary reference point for non-Euclidean geometry in horror writing. What did Lovecraft call the geometry of R'lyeh in the story?
answer: 'Loathsomely redolent of spheres and dimensions apart from ours'
choices: 'Loathsomely redolent of spheres and dimensions apart from ours'
'Made of corners that opened sideways from sanity itself'
'A geometry of impossible curvature that bent the gaze of the beholder'
'Carved against the laws of Euclid by a mathematics older than men'
context: Lovecraft had been reading popular accounts of Einstein and Riemann throughout the 1920s. His 1928 phrase 'spheres and dimensions apart from ours' was a science-aware way of conveying that R'lyeh's geometry obeyed rules incompatible with our spacetime. The Emma's voyage starts in New Zealand in March 1925 and ends with Johansen alone, surviving to write the manuscript in Oslo. The story's three-part structure — the professor's papers, the New Orleans cult raid, and the Norwegian's account — gives it a documentary feel Lovecraft would refine throughout his career.

question: Tolkien wrote 'The Riddles in the Dark' chapter of The Hobbit in 1932, in its first published form. In that original 1937 version, Gollum was less monstrous — and the chapter's logic, structure, and outcome were noticeably different from what readers know today. Tolkien rewrote the chapter substantially in 1947 to make it consistent with the just-completed Lord of the Rings, in which the Ring needed to be a sinister object Gollum would never willingly give away. The most important plot change between the 1937 and 1947 versions of the chapter centered on what?
answer: In 1937 Gollum cheerfully offered the Ring as the prize for losing the riddle game; in 1947 Tolkien rewrote it so Gollum lied and tried to murder Bilbo when he lost
choices: In 1937 Gollum cheerfully offered the Ring as the prize for losing the riddle game; in 1947 Tolkien rewrote it so Gollum lied and tried to murder Bilbo when he lost
In 1937 the cave was located in the Misty Mountains; in 1947 Tolkien moved it to the Iron Hills
In 1937 Bilbo defeated Gollum in single combat; in 1947 Tolkien revised the contest to a true riddle exchange
In 1937 Gollum had no name; in 1947 Tolkien gave him the Sméagol backstory and the river-folk origin
context: Tolkien justified the 1947 rewrite as a textual correction — within the in-story conceit, Bilbo had originally told the Riddles chapter wrongly in the Red Book of Westmarch, then later told the true version to Frodo and Gandalf. The 1951 second edition of The Hobbit reflects this rewrite; copies of the 1937 first edition with the original benign Gollum are extremely valuable to collectors. Tolkien himself wrote in a 1959 letter that the original chapter 'gave a wholly different impression of the chief character.'

question: Robert E. Howard's Conan stories ran in Weird Tales from December 1932 until October 1936 — twenty-one stories total. The very last Conan story Howard wrote before his suicide in June 1936 was a novel-length work, not a magazine story. It was rejected by every major magazine of the era and only saw print posthumously, in serialized form, in Weird Tales over the December 1935 through April 1936 issues — the final months of Howard's life. The novel introduced the Black Stone of Set, the ancient sorcerer Thoth-Amon, and the desperate Aquilonian king Conan in the most directly political of the Conan stories. What was the novel titled?
answer: The Hour of the Dragon (later republished as Conan the Conqueror)
choices: The Hour of the Dragon (later republished as Conan the Conqueror)
The Phoenix on the Sword (the original Conan debut)
Beyond the Black River (the frontier-Pictish horror)
context: Hour of the Dragon was Howard's only full-length Conan novel. He wrote it in late 1934 and early 1935 specifically to crack the British hardcover market, which Weird Tales editor Farnsworth Wright had urged him to pursue. The novel was rejected by every house. The serialization in Weird Tales' final months of Howard's life (Dec 1935 - Apr 1936) was its first publication. Gnome Press's 1950 republication as Conan the Conqueror was the first hardback Conan. Frazetta's painting for the 1967 Lancer paperback edition is the iconic Conan-on-throne image.

question: August Derleth and Donald Wandrei founded Arkham House in October 1939 with a single specific purpose: to keep H.P. Lovecraft's work in print after Lovecraft's 1937 death. The press's first publication, in November 1939, was a thick hardback collection of Lovecraft's best stories, edited from Lovecraft's manuscripts in Sonia Greene's possession. The print run was small. Each copy sold at a price comparable to a paperback today — but most went unsold for years; copies sat in Derleth's Sauk City basement until the late 1940s. The print run of the first edition was tiny enough that surviving copies are now among the most valuable horror books on the market. What was the original print run of Arkham House's first publication?
context: The Outsider and Others (1939) was 553 pages. Derleth and Wandrei calculated they needed about 1,268 sales to break even at the $3.50 cover price. They financed the print run from their own pockets — Derleth had small royalties from his Wisconsin regional novels, and Wandrei was a stockbroker. By the 1990s, mint first-edition copies were selling for over $5,000; in the 2010s, signed copies reached $10,000+. Arkham House remained continuously in operation under Derleth, his son April Derleth, and current ownership.

question: Philip K. Dick's 1968 novel Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? was bought by Ridley Scott's team for a Hollywood adaptation in the late 1970s. Hampton Fancher and David Peoples wrote the screenplay. Dick was suspicious of the project — until he saw a 20-minute rough cut at Warner Bros. in October 1981 and was deeply moved. He died of stroke in Santa Ana on March 2, 1982, three months before the film's June release. The film's iconic 'Tears in Rain' monologue, spoken by Rutger Hauer as the dying replicant Roy Batty, was rewritten by Hauer himself on the night before shooting. What 1996 biographer recorded Hauer's full account of writing the speech?
answer: Paul M. Sammon, author of Future Noir
choices: Paul M. Sammon, author of Future Noir
Jerry Pournelle, in his Galaxy column
Roger Ebert, in his 1992 Great Movies
Pauline Kael, in the 1982 New Yorker
context: Sammon's Future Noir (1996, revised 2007) remains the definitive making-of book on Blade Runner. Hauer reduced what was a longer scripted speech to its iconic core: 'I've seen things you people wouldn't believe. Attack ships on fire off the shoulder of Orion. I watched C-beams glitter in the dark near the Tannhäuser Gate. All those moments will be lost in time, like tears in rain. Time to die.' The original script lines (which Hauer kept) were technical descriptions of off-world warfare; Hauer transmuted them into poetry. Ridley Scott has called it the single most moving line ever written for him.

question: The Silmarillion, published by Christopher Tolkien in 1977 four years after his father's death, is the central mythological background to all of Tolkien's Middle-earth fiction. The book's First Age narrative centers on three holy jewels — the Silmarils — wrought by the Elf-king Fëanor of the Noldor in Valinor. The Silmarils contain the light of the Two Trees of Valinor before they were destroyed. Each gem's particular quality is what makes them irreplaceable. They are stolen by the first Dark Lord (Morgoth, Sauron's master), set into his iron crown, and become the focus of three Ages of war. What specifically did Fëanor put into the Silmarils that no other gem ever made could contain?
answer: The light of the Two Trees of Valinor (Telperion and Laurelin), captured before the Trees were destroyed by Morgoth and Ungoliant
choices: The light of the Two Trees of Valinor (Telperion and Laurelin), captured before the Trees were destroyed by Morgoth and Ungoliant
The first stars Varda had kindled in the sky during the elves' awakening at Cuiviénen
A drop of the blood of the Vala Aulë, shed during the forging of the Dwarven Seven Fathers
The compressed essence of Eru Ilúvatar's first creative thought before the Music of the Ainur
context: The Two Trees of Valinor were the original source of light in Tolkien's cosmos, made by Yavanna at the beginning of the world. Telperion was silver, Laurelin gold. Morgoth (Melkor, the first Dark Lord) allied with the great spider Ungoliant to destroy them, drinking their light into her void. Fëanor's three Silmarils contained the only surviving light of the Two Trees. After Morgoth's defeat at the end of the First Age, one Silmaril rises into the heavens as the morning/evening star Eärendil; the other two are cast into the sea and the earth by Maedhros and Maglor.

question: Tolkien's friend C.S. Lewis converted from atheism to Christianity (specifically, to Anglicanism) in 1931 after a long evening walk and conversation with Tolkien and Hugo Dyson along Addison's Walk at Magdalen College, Oxford on the night of September 19, 1931. The conversation centered on Tolkien's argument that the pagan myths Lewis loved — Balder, Adonis, the death-and-resurrection patterns — were 'splintered lights' pointing toward the one true myth that had actually happened in history. Tolkien recorded this conversation in a poem Lewis cited as personally important in his religious thought. What was that 1931 Tolkien poem titled?
choices: The Lay of Aotrou and Itroun
context: Mythopoeia is a 148-line poem written for Lewis. Its key argument: man is a 'sub-creator' bearing 'the refracted Light through whom is splintered from a single White / to many hues, and endlessly combined / in living shapes that move from mind to mind.' Lewis's account of the conversation is in Surprised by Joy (1955) and in a letter to Arthur Greeves dated 18 October 1931. Lewis converted to theism in 1929 and to Christianity specifically after the Addison's Walk conversation. Mythopoeia was published posthumously in Tree and Leaf (1964) with 'On Fairy-Stories' and 'Leaf by Niggle.'

question: Edgar Allan Poe's 1849 death in Baltimore on October 7 remains the most-discussed literary death in American history. He was found four days earlier — October 3 — outside Ryan's Tavern at 4th and Lombard, delirious, wearing someone else's clothes (a cheap stained suit, not the formal black he had been seen in days before), unable to explain who had clothed him or where he had been. He was taken to Washington College Hospital. Over four days of fever and delirium, he refused to drink alcohol though it was offered. He repeatedly called out one name — Reynolds — that no biographer has ever conclusively identified. He died early on October 7, aged 40. The leading modern theory, advanced by which figure in 1996, holds that Poe died of an animal-borne illness incompatible with the supposedly drunken state in which he had been found?
answer: Dr. R. Michael Benitez, the University of Maryland cardiologist who proposed rabies as the cause
choices: Dr. R. Michael Benitez, the University of Maryland cardiologist who proposed rabies as the cause
Dr. John Carlson, the medical historian who proposed encephalitis
Dr. Marie-Claude Caron, the French academic who proposed brain tumor
Dr. Peter Kennedy, the Edinburgh neurologist who proposed Lyme disease
context: Benitez presented the rabies hypothesis at a 1996 medical history conference and published it in the Maryland Medical Journal. His argument: Poe's symptoms (delirium, hydrophobia-like aversion to drink, perspiration, hallucinations) match rabies's presentation; alcoholism alone does not explain the four days of symptoms before death. Competing theories include cooping (election-day kidnapping for repeated voting), brain tumor, syphilis tertiary, and heavy-metal poisoning. The mystery of who clothed Poe, where he had been, and who 'Reynolds' was remains unsolved.

question: John W. Campbell, editing Astounding Science-Fiction from 1937 through 1971, published in the August 1938 issue a novella that became the basis for two classic Hollywood films — Howard Hawks's 1951 The Thing from Another World and John Carpenter's 1982 The Thing. Campbell wrote the novella himself under his Don A. Stuart pseudonym. The story is set at a fictional Antarctic research station. Twelve men discover a frozen alien spacecraft and the still-frozen body of its pilot, which they thaw out in the lab. The alien turns out to be a shape-shifting predator. The novella's title literally asks the sentry's challenge; what does that title phrase reveal about the survivors' climactic problem?
answer: Asks 'Who Goes There?' — by the climax no one can tell who is human and who is the alien wearing a human's face
choices: Asks 'Who Goes There?' — by the climax no one can tell who is human and who is the alien wearing a human's face
Asks 'Who Goes There?' — the alien is identified by being unable to give the proper sentry response in English
Asks 'Who Goes There?' — the alien is detected when it answers incorrectly in clipped Norwegian dialect
Asks 'Who Goes There?' — the alien is found out when it cannot reply with the radio operator's call sign
context: Campbell's central horror is that the alien perfectly imitates whatever it consumes, including memory and personality. By the climax, the survivors devise a blood test: each man's blood is drawn and given an electric current; the alien-blood will react to defend itself. Carpenter's 1982 film made this test the centerpiece scene. The 1951 Hawks film simplifies the shape-shifting concept; Carpenter's is the closer adaptation. Bill Lancaster wrote Carpenter's screenplay; Ennio Morricone scored the film.

question: Tolkien's Lord of the Rings was published in three volumes by George Allen & Unwin in London between July 1954 and October 1955. Tolkien had wanted a single-volume publication; the publisher split it for economic reasons (paper shortages were lingering from postwar rationing) and to share risk across three smaller print runs. Tolkien resisted the volume titles his publisher proposed; he eventually accepted them under protest. Tolkien himself would have called the three volumes by what alternative titles, drawing on his text's natural divisions?
answer: The Ring Sets Out, The Ring Goes South, and The Ring Goes East — his proposed volume titles matching the three internal Book divisions
choices: The Ring Sets Out, The Ring Goes South, and The Ring Goes East — his proposed volume titles matching the three internal Book divisions
The Shadow Grows, The Eye of the Enemy, and The Return of the King — names that match the three Sauron-encounter phases
Mordor in Sight, Mordor Approached, and Mordor Entered — names that emphasize the Frodo plot specifically
Hobbiton, Lothlórien, and Gondor — names that emphasize the principal setting of each volume's first chapter
context: Tolkien's preferred volume titles followed the six internal 'Books' the novel is divided into: Books I-II were 'The Ring Sets Out,' Books III-IV 'The Ring Goes South' (later 'The Treason of Isengard' in one variant), and Books V-VI 'The Ring Goes East' (sometimes 'The War of the Ring' / 'The Return of the King'). The published titles — Fellowship, Two Towers, Return of the King — were Rayner Unwin's. Tolkien complained in letters that 'The Two Towers' was particularly ambiguous (which two towers? he could name at least four candidate pairs). The publisher won the argument; the published titles became standard.

question: Lord Dunsany — Edward Plunkett, 18th Baron Dunsany, 1878-1957 — was the single most important literary influence on the early Lovecraft and a major influence on Tolkien. His 1905 prose-poem collection of invented mythology was Lovecraft's primary stylistic template for his Dream Cycle stories. Dunsany wrote in a deliberately archaic, scriptural prose modeled on the King James Bible. He was an Anglo-Irish Protestant, a regular at Yeats's Dublin circle, and a Boer War / WWI veteran. His 1924 fantasy novel about a king's son and an elven princess is widely considered his masterpiece. What was that 1924 novel called?
choices: The Curse of the Wise Woman
context: The King of Elfland's Daughter combines the medieval romance form with mystical fantasy, directly anticipating Tolkien's Smith of Wootton Major and parts of The Silmarillion. Lord Dunsany held the peerage at Dunsany Castle, Co. Meath, Ireland (the castle has been in his family since the 1180s — still inhabited by Dunsanys today). Dunsany was a championship-class chess player who once drew with the Cuban world champion Capablanca. He survived the burning of Dunsany Castle during the Irish War of Independence. Tolkien wrote that Dunsany's Gods of Pegana 'made me realize a writer could create a religion from nothing.'

question: Philip K. Dick experienced a series of religious-mystical events in February and March 1974 — what he called the '2-3-74 experiences' — that consumed the rest of his life and shaped his last six novels. Dick spent the next eight years writing an enormous private journal of philosophical speculation about what had happened to him. The journal eventually ran over 8,000 pages. A selection was published posthumously in 2011, twenty-nine years after Dick's death. What was the published selection called?
answer: The Exegesis of Philip K. Dick
choices: The Exegesis of Philip K. Dick
context: The Exegesis is over 1,000,000 words in total. The 2011 published selection (edited by Pamela Jackson and Jonathan Lethem) ran 944 pages, a 10% selection of the available archive. Dick's experience began with a delivery driver wearing a Christian fish-symbol necklace; from there Dick believed he was receiving 'pink light' transmissions from a Vast Active Living Intelligence System (VALIS). His diagnoses ran from schizophrenia to temporal lobe epilepsy to vitamin overdose to genuine gnostic revelation, depending on his mood. Dick died in March 1982 in Santa Ana, California, of a stroke.

question: Tolkien's Middle-earth mythology began as private writing during WWI. The earliest surviving fragments are pencil drafts in notebooks he kept while recovering from trench fever in late 1916. One of the very first stories he drafted was the tragic doomed love between an elf-maiden and a mortal man — the seed of what became the Beren and Lúthien legend. In 1917, in Roos Wood, Yorkshire, Tolkien's wife Edith danced for him among the hemlock blossoms; he immediately connected the moment to his story. What names appear on the joint Tolkien gravestone in Wolvercote Cemetery, Oxford?
choices: Galadriel and Celeborn, the immortal couple
Arwen and Aragorn, the mortal-elven pair
Eärendil and Elwing, the lovers of the Sea
context: Edith Bratt had been Tolkien's secret fiancée since his teens. After his hospitalization in late 1916 with trench fever, Edith danced for him among the hemlock blooms of Roos Wood in East Yorkshire. They married March 22, 1916 (before his deployment to France). Edith died November 29, 1971; J.R.R. died September 2, 1973. Their joint grave in Wolvercote Cemetery, North Oxford bears the names Christopher Tolkien arranged: 'Edith Mary Tolkien, Lúthien, 1889-1971' and 'John Ronald Reuel Tolkien, Beren, 1892-1973.'

question: On August 15, 1977, the Big Ear radio telescope at Ohio State University, operated by Jerry Ehman, recorded a 72-second signal at the 1420 MHz hydrogen-line frequency, coming from the direction of the constellation Sagittarius. The signal was 30 times louder than the background noise. Ehman saw it on the computer printout days later and wrote a single comment in the margin in red pen. The signal has never been detected again despite repeated searches. In the world of SETI and pulp-era cosmic-mystery overlap, it remains the most analyzed unexplained narrowband radio transmission in history. What did Ehman write in the margin?
context: The 'Wow! Signal' has driven 47+ years of SETI follow-up observations. The 1420 MHz frequency is significant because hydrogen — the most common element in the universe — naturally radiates at it; a civilization wanting to be heard would choose 1420 MHz. The Big Ear telescope itself was demolished in 1998 to make way for a golf course. Ehman remained skeptical the signal was extraterrestrial but never reached a confirmed natural explanation. Antonio Paris in 2017 proposed it might have been from a comet, but the comet hypothesis was challenged by follow-up observations. The signal sits alongside the Roswell incident (1947), Patterson-Gimlin (1967), DB Cooper (1971), and Mothman (1966-67) in the pulp-fiction-adjacent canon of unexplained American mysteries.

question: Hal Foster's medieval-knight comic strip launched in 1937 and ran continuously in Sunday newspapers for over 80 years. The hero is a young Norse prince from Thule who joins King Arthur's Round Table and eventually marries an Asian princess named Aleta. Foster's hand-drawn art is considered one of the finest in comics history. What's the strip called?
context: Foster drew Prince Valiant himself from February 1937 until 1971. The strip is set in 5th-century Arthurian Britain but ranges across Europe, Africa, and even North America. King Features Syndicate distributes it. Foster had previously drawn the Tarzan Sunday strip from 1931 to 1937 before launching Valiant as his own creation. Aleta of the Misty Isles becomes Val's wife in 1946.

question: Lee Falk created a costumed jungle vigilante in 1936, considered the first hero in a purple bodysuit and domino mask. The character lives in a Skull Cave deep in the African jungle and is treated as immortal by the natives — but in fact each generation passes the mantle to his son. What's the character called?
context: The Phantom debuted in newspaper strips on February 17, 1936 — predating Superman (1938) by two years, making him arguably the first costumed superhero. Lee Falk also created Mandrake the Magician (1934). The current Phantom is the 21st in line. The Skull Cave is in the fictional African country of Bangalla. Native tribes call him 'the Ghost Who Walks.'

question: Edgar Allan Poe wrote what may be the most famous detective story of the 19th century in 1844 — a story about a stolen letter the Paris police cannot find despite ransacking the suspect's apartment. Dupin solves the case by realizing the letter has been hidden in plain sight on the suspect's mantelpiece, casually inverted and re-addressed. The story has become a touchstone in literary theory after Lacan and Derrida famously debated its meaning. What's the story called?
choices: The Murders in the Rue Morgue
context: Published in The Gift annual in 1844. The 'Minister D—' steals a compromising letter from the Queen and hides it in plain sight; Dupin recovers it. Jacques Lacan's 1956 seminar on the story and Jacques Derrida's response ('Le facteur de la vérité') are landmark texts of post-structuralist literary theory. Borges, Eco, and Auster have all written homage-stories. The phrase 'hiding in plain sight' is sometimes credited to Poe.

question: Tolkien's posthumous collection The Father Christmas Letters (1976) gathers letters Tolkien wrote to his own children from 1920 to 1943, each ostensibly from Father Christmas at the North Pole. The letters include illustrations and a running cast of characters at the North Pole — a clumsy assistant, polar bears, gnomes. What's the chief North Pole goblin's name in Tolkien's letters?
choices: Snow Bear (the rival of Father Christmas)
context: Tolkien wrote the letters for his children John, Michael, Christopher, and Priscilla. Polar Bear is the clumsy disaster-prone assistant whose mishaps drive most of the letter-plots. Father Christmas himself writes in shaky red ink (Tolkien's annotation: 'I have written this with a Polar Bear paw'). Tolkien hand-illustrated each letter. Baillie Tolkien (Christopher's second wife) edited the published collection in 1976. The 1999 'centenary' expanded edition added previously unseen letters.

question: Conan Doyle's Sherlock Holmes — debuted in A Study in Scarlet (1887) — was widely seen as a direct descendant of Poe's Dupin. Doyle freely acknowledged Poe's influence in his autobiography Memories and Adventures (1924). But Doyle also based Holmes physically and intellectually on a specific real Edinburgh medical professor whose deductive teaching of physical-symptom diagnosis stunned the young Doyle. Doyle had been the professor's clinical clerk in 1877-78. The professor's deductive demonstrations — pinpointing a patient's profession, region, illness, and recent travels from a single glance — were the template for Holmes. Who was he?
context: Joseph Bell (1837-1911) was Royal Edinburgh Infirmary's consulting surgeon and a lecturer at Edinburgh Medical School. He took Doyle as a clinical clerk in 1877. Bell's teaching method: a patient enters the lecture room; Bell deduces occupation, hometown, recent travel, and illness from physical evidence (calluses, sunburn, accent, gait); only then takes the formal history. Doyle wrote to Bell in 1892 acknowledging him as Holmes's model. The Edinburgh detective Hercule Poirot was modeled on a different real Belgian refugee Christie knew.

question: Robert E. Howard's 'Beyond the Black River' (Weird Tales, May-June 1935) is widely considered Howard's finest single Conan story. Set on the Pictish frontier of Aquilonia, the story is essentially a Western with Picts in place of Apaches. Conan and the Aquilonian forester Balthus must defend a frontier fort from a Pictish raid led by a shaman who commands the night and the rivers. Howard told a friend in a 1935 letter that he had based the story explicitly on real American frontier history — specifically, a 1790s war in which one tribe nearly destroyed white settlement of the Ohio Valley. Which historical episode was Howard's model?
answer: The Northwest Indian War of 1785-1795, fought between the U.S. and the Western Confederacy
choices: The Northwest Indian War of 1785-1795, fought between the U.S. and the Western Confederacy
The Powhatan Wars of 1610-1646 in early colonial Virginia
Bacon's Rebellion of 1676 against William Berkeley in Virginia
The Seminole Wars of 1817-1858 in the Florida swamps
context: Howard had been reading the American historian Allan W. Eckert's pre-publication research; he was particularly fascinated by Little Turtle's 1791 victory over General St. Clair (more Americans died at St. Clair's Defeat than at Custer's Last Stand). 'Beyond the Black River' is the only Conan story without supernatural elements until the climax. Howard intended the story as a meditation on civilization's fragile margins: 'Barbarism is the natural state of mankind. Civilization is unnatural — a whim of circumstance.'

question: Edgar Rice Burroughs invented multiple lost-world franchises beyond Tarzan and John Carter. His 1918 magazine serial about a captured German U-boat captain and a stranded American who discover a primordial island in the South Pacific where evolutionary stages of life are spatially distributed (early stages in the south, modern stages in the north) inspired the 1975 Amicus film series. The island has a peculiar geographical feature — a single navigable river running through impassable cliffs. What did Burroughs call the lost island?
context: The Caspak trilogy comprises The Land That Time Forgot (1918), The People That Time Forgot (1918), and Out of Time's Abyss (1918), all originally serialized in Blue Book Magazine. Caspak's spatial-evolutionary scheme — life evolves as it migrates north — is one of pulp's most original cosmologies. The 1975 Kevin Connor film adaptation The Land That Time Forgot starred Doug McClure. Maple White Land is the setting of Conan Doyle's The Lost World (1912); Skull Island is King Kong's home.

question: Tolkien's Catholic faith shaped his fiction at every level. He converted his fiancée Edith Bratt from Anglicanism to Catholicism in 1913 (she resented this for decades). He attended daily Mass for most of his adult life. He famously wrote in a 1953 letter that The Lord of the Rings was 'fundamentally religious and Catholic' — but also that he had 'cut out practically all references to anything like religion' so as not to embarrass the story with explicit allegory. Tolkien wrote a Modern English translation of which Old English Catholic devotional text — one of the very few poetic works he completed for publication?
choices: Caedmon's Hymn, the earliest known Old English poem
The Dream of the Rood, the cross-as-narrator Crucifixion poem
Christ III, the Cynewulf eschatological poem
context: Tolkien's translation of Pearl (along with Sir Gawain and the Green Knight and Sir Orfeo) was published posthumously by Christopher Tolkien in 1975. Pearl is by the same anonymous 14th-century Pearl Poet who wrote Sir Gawain. The poem features a grieving father who has lost his two-year-old daughter and dreams of meeting her, now a grown maiden in heavenly bliss. The Pearl Poet's other surviving works are Sir Gawain and the Green Knight (Tolkien co-edited the standard scholarly edition with E.V. Gordon, 1925) and Patience and Cleanness.

question: T.H. White's 1958 single-volume omnibus The Once and Future King combined four previously separate novels (The Sword in the Stone, 1938; The Queen of Air and Darkness, 1939, originally The Witch in the Wood; The Ill-Made Knight, 1940; The Candle in the Wind, 1958) into the most-read 20th-century Arthurian work. The novels follow Arthur from boyhood (under Merlyn's tutelage) through old age. White began work in 1936, paused during WWII, and finally combined and revised the volumes in 1958. The 1960 Broadway musical adapted from the first volume gave the franchise its now-iconic name. What was the musical called?
context: Camelot opened at Toronto's O'Keefe Centre in October 1960, then moved to Broadway. Music by Frederick Loewe, lyrics by Alan Jay Lerner. The original cast featured Richard Burton as Arthur, Julie Andrews as Guenevere, and Robert Goulet as Lancelot. The Kennedy White House famously associated itself with the show — Jackie Kennedy named the Kennedy administration 'Camelot' in a Life magazine interview a week after JFK's assassination. The 1967 film starred Richard Harris, Vanessa Redgrave, and Franco Nero.

question: Sir Thomas Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur, completed around 1469-70 and first printed by William Caxton in 1485, is the single most important medieval Arthurian text. It compiles French Vulgate and Post-Vulgate sources plus original English material into a unified narrative covering the rise of Arthur, the Grail quest, the love of Lancelot and Guenevere, and the fall of the Round Table. Malory wrote it while imprisoned in Newgate Prison. He had been convicted of which series of unusual crimes that put him in repeated trouble through the 1450s and 1460s?
answer: Theft, robbery, attempted murder, rape, and cattle-raiding
choices: Theft, robbery, attempted murder, rape, and cattle-raiding
Heresy, treason against Edward IV, and Lollard sympathies
Piracy in the English Channel and Welsh smuggling
Counterfeiting royal coin and forging episcopal documents
context: Malory's biography is reconstructed mainly from court records. He was knight of Newbold Revel in Warwickshire, served in the French campaigns under Henry V's son, then turned to local-level criminality in the 1450s. The 1469-70 Newgate imprisonment was his final and longest. He died in March 1471 and was buried at Greyfriars near Newgate. Caxton's 1485 printed edition imposed the title 'Le Morte d'Arthur' (Malory had called the work 'The Hoole Book of Kyng Arthur and of His Noble Knyghtes of the Rounde Table'). The 1934 Winchester Manuscript discovery doubled Malory scholarship.

question: Asimov's first published robot story, 'Robbie' (originally 'Strange Playfellow' in Super Science Stories, September 1940), introduced his Three Laws — though they were not formally stated until 'Runaround' (Astounding, March 1942). In 1985, four decades into his career, Asimov added a Zeroth Law that supersedes the original three. He introduced it in the novel that united his Robot, Empire, and Foundation series into a single timeline. The novel's plot turns on the robot R. Daneel Olivaw realizing the Three Laws are insufficient to protect humanity as a whole, leading him to articulate the higher principle. What novel introduced the Zeroth Law, and what does it state?
answer: Robots and Empire (1985) — 'A robot may not harm humanity, or by inaction allow humanity to come to harm'
choices: Robots and Empire (1985) — 'A robot may not harm humanity, or by inaction allow humanity to come to harm'
Foundation and Earth (1986) — 'A robot must protect the long-term flourishing of all human society'
The Robots of Dawn (1983) — 'A robot must place collective good above individual welfare'
Forward the Foundation (1993) — 'A robot may serve humanity even at the cost of an individual'
context: Robots and Empire was the 1985 bridge novel. R. Daneel (introduced in The Caves of Steel, 1954) and R. Giskard (in The Robots of Dawn, 1983) realize they must extend the First Law beyond individual humans. Giskard articulates the Zeroth Law and immediately positronic-burns out — the strain of overriding the original First Law destroys him. Daneel carries the Zeroth Law forward into the Foundation series, ultimately becoming the secret architect of Hari Seldon's psychohistory.

question: H.P. Lovecraft died March 15, 1937 in Providence's Jane Brown Memorial Hospital. He had been keeping a detailed clinical journal of his own symptoms — intestinal cancer plus Bright's disease — because the medical observation interested him. He had refused painkillers so his mind would remain clear for his observations. His final letter, written about two weeks before death, went to a young writer he had been mentoring through correspondence — a Wisconsin author who would, two years later, co-found Arkham House specifically to save Lovecraft's work from oblivion. Lovecraft's death certificate gave his net worth as approximately $25. The Wisconsin correspondent traveled to Providence in 1939 to retrieve manuscripts from Lovecraft's widow Sonia. Who was he?
context: Derleth (1909-1971) was 28 when Lovecraft died. He had been corresponding with Lovecraft since 1926 and had sold his own first story to Weird Tales at 17. Derleth's Sauk City, Wisconsin life was anchored in regional Midwestern fiction (his Sac Prairie Saga ran to dozens of novels). With Donald Wandrei (Lovecraft's other devoted New England correspondent), Derleth founded Arkham House in October 1939 specifically to publish The Outsider and Others. The press has been continuously operating ever since. Derleth's own pastiche-mythos stories drew criticism for systematizing what Lovecraft had left ambiguous.

question: Tolkien's Anglo-Saxon scholarship was profoundly serious. His 1936 British Academy lecture 'Beowulf: The Monsters and the Critics' transformed academic Beowulf studies by arguing the poem should be read as a coherent literary work, not as a quarry for historical data. Tolkien argued that the dragon Grendel and the unnamed final dragon were the heart of the poem's meaning — not mere narrative ornament. The lecture's central claim was that Anglo-Saxon literature is built on a particular tragic-heroic worldview that Tolkien named with a specific term he traced to Old English. What was that term?
answer: The Northern courage of resistance — fighting on though the cause is hopeless and defeat is certain
choices: The Northern courage of resistance — fighting on though the cause is hopeless and defeat is certain
The Anglo-Saxon doctrine of wyrd — fate as the ultimate arbiter of all human endeavor
The Heroic Code of dryht — the warband loyalty above family or kin
The Pagan-Germanic concept of doom — the certainty of cosmic destruction at Ragnarok
context: Tolkien's central argument: Norse-Germanic heroism is unique in world literature for celebrating defiance in the face of certain loss. The hero knows the world will end (Ragnarök / Doomsday); knows he himself will die; nevertheless fights on, because that is what a man does. Tolkien contrasted this with the Greek heroic code (where the hero hopes for posthumous glory) and the Christian one (where the hero hopes for resurrection). The 'Northern theory of courage' shapes Théoden's last stand, Aragorn at the Black Gate, Frodo's hopeless climb, and Sam's mantra ('There's some good in this world, Mr. Frodo, and it's worth fighting for').

question: Howard's correspondence with Lovecraft from 1930 to 1936 totals roughly 600,000 words across 200 letters, preserved largely thanks to August Derleth and the Howard Memorial Museum. The two writers debated civilization-vs-barbarism, the New England weird tradition vs. the Texas frontier tradition, race-and-nation theory, and the proper aesthetics of pulp. Their fundamental disagreement was philosophical. In a famous May 1936 letter — written just six weeks before Howard's suicide — Howard summarized his position as follows: 'I am not what could be called a civilized man. I have always preferred...' The completion of that line became one of Howard's most-quoted statements. What did he prefer?
answer: '...the barbarian to the civilized man, because the barbarian is at base a free man'
choices: '...the barbarian to the civilized man, because the barbarian is at base a free man'
'...the Texas frontier to the New England library, however erudite or sheltered'
'...the open Sun and the open Plain to the closed room and the dusty book'
'...the man who works with his hands to the man who works only with his pen'
context: Howard's full passage to Lovecraft: 'Barbarism is the natural state of mankind. Civilization is unnatural — it is a whim of circumstance. And barbarism must always ultimately triumph.' Lovecraft's response (Lovecraft's letters to Howard generally ran twice as long as Howard's to him) argued that civilization was a fragile but indispensable achievement and that barbarism was identical to slavery, not freedom. The Howard-Lovecraft correspondence is preserved in two-volume scholarly editions; selected letters are reprinted in the 2007 Hippocampus Press collection. Howard committed suicide on June 11, 1936.

question: Mary Stewart's Merlin Trilogy (The Crystal Cave, 1970; The Hollow Hills, 1973; The Last Enchantment, 1979) retold the Arthurian story from Merlin's perspective. Stewart drew on the 9th-century Welsh Historia Brittonum, Geoffrey of Monmouth's 1136 History of the Kings of Britain (which invented most of the Arthurian framework Western tradition received), and the 12th-13th-century French Vulgate Cycle. Stewart's Merlin is a half-divine illegitimate child raised in 5th-century Wales after the Roman withdrawal. The trilogy's title (and the trilogy's setting) refers to a real geological feature in Wales — a coastal site historically associated with Merlin's youth. Where is the actual Crystal Cave?
answer: Bryn Myrddin near Carmarthen in southwest Wales, the legendary home of Myrddin Wyllt, the Welsh Merlin
choices: Bryn Myrddin near Carmarthen in southwest Wales, the legendary home of Myrddin Wyllt, the Welsh Merlin
Cadbury Castle in Somerset, the leading archaeological candidate for the historical Camelot
Tintagel Castle on the Cornish coast, the traditional birthplace of Arthur in Geoffrey of Monmouth
Glastonbury Tor in Somerset, the leading candidate for the location of the Isle of Avalon
context: Carmarthen (Welsh: Caerfyrddin = 'Fort of Myrddin') is on Wales's southwest coast. The Welsh tradition of Myrddin Wyllt (Wild Myrddin) predates Geoffrey of Monmouth by centuries — Myrddin appears in 6th-century Welsh poetry as a battle-bard who lost his mind after the Battle of Arfderydd (573 AD). Geoffrey's 1136 History conflated Myrddin with a similar figure named Ambrosius and Latinized the name as Merlinus. Stewart visited Carmarthen and Wales extensively while writing the trilogy. Her later Mary Stewart trilogy The Wicked Day (1983) follows Mordred. The combined four-book sequence is sometimes called the Arthurian Saga.

question: Marion Zimmer Bradley's 1983 novel The Mists of Avalon retold the Arthurian legend from the perspective of the women — Igraine, Morgaine (Morgan le Fay), Morgause, Viviane (the Lady of the Lake), and Gwenhwyfar. Bradley framed the Arthurian conflict as a religious war between matriarchal pre-Christian goddess-worship (centered at the holy island of Avalon, increasingly fading into the mists) and the encroaching patriarchal Christianity. The novel was a massive commercial success and a major touchstone for 1980s feminist fantasy. Bradley's posthumous public reputation collapsed in the 2010s after her daughter Moira Greyland published what specific account in 2014?
answer: An autobiographical account confirming that Bradley had sexually abused her daughter and other children for decades while writing the matriarchal-feminist novels
choices: An autobiographical account confirming that Bradley had sexually abused her daughter and other children for decades while writing the matriarchal-feminist novels
A scholarly study arguing Bradley's Avalon novels had appropriated Welsh oral tradition without scholarly attribution
A literary biography revealing Bradley had not actually written the later Avalon series volumes herself
A memoir describing the Bradley household's involvement in 1970s Berkeley cult activity
context: Moira Greyland's account (published in The Last Closet, 2017, after Bradley's death) confirmed long-standing rumors and made explicit that Bradley had been a sexual predator. Bradley's husband Walter Breen had been convicted of child molestation in 1990. The revelations have led many readers to reassess the matriarchal religious framework of the Avalon novels — which had presented child-rearing and inter-generational female knowledge transmission as the highest moral good while the author was perpetrating its opposite. The case has become a textbook example in literature-and-ethics teaching.

question: Robert E. Howard's complete Conan canon — 21 stories Howard wrote before his June 1936 suicide — was a foundational influence on dozens of later writers. The single most influential post-Howard fantasy-writing duo took Conan as their model when launching their own bestselling series in the 1970s — a series of novels about an exiled Earthman who becomes a barbarian warlord on a primitive planet, all written in deliberate imitation of Howard's prose rhythms. The duo wrote 17 collaborative novels in the cycle from 1971 to 1991. Who were they?
answer: Andrew J. Offutt with Karl Edward Wagner
choices: Andrew J. Offutt with Karl Edward Wagner
L. Sprague de Camp with Lin Carter
context: L. Sprague de Camp and Lin Carter were the post-Howard Conan continuators — co-editors of the 1966-1971 Lancer Conan paperbacks with Frazetta covers. De Camp wrote the 1953 Tales of Conan (the first Conan collection to add new pastiche material). Carter and de Camp also co-wrote the 1968-1977 Thongor and 1973 Kothar series. Andrew J. Offutt and Karl Edward Wagner separately edited the Year's Best Horror Stories series, but never co-wrote a barbarian series. The exiled-Earthman-on-primitive-planet motif fits John Norman's controversial Gor series, not the Conan continuation.

question: Robert Heinlein wrote Stranger in a Strange Land between 1948 and 1960. He had been thinking about the central idea since the late 1940s — a Martian-raised human raised by Martians and returned to Earth as an adult. The novel was finally published by Putnam in June 1961 after every other publisher had rejected its length and content. It became a counterculture touchstone in the 1960s; Charles Manson supposedly drew on parts of it. Heinlein's protagonist Valentine Michael Smith founds a religious movement on Earth based on Martian principles. Smith's followers learn to deeply understand things through total empathic absorption. What Martian word did Heinlein invent for this concept — a word that subsequently entered the English language?
context: 'Grok' literally means 'to drink' in the Martian language Heinlein invented for the novel — but conceptually means understanding so thoroughly that the observer becomes part of the observed. The word entered the OED in 2002. Silicon Valley engineers adopted it widely in the 1970s; you can still find it in the Jargon File. The novel won the 1962 Hugo Award. Heinlein dedicated it to Robert Cornog, Frederik Brown, and Phil Farmer. The original 220,000-word manuscript was 60,000 words longer than the 1961 published version; the full original was finally released in 1991 as Stranger in a Strange Land: The Uncut Edition.

question: Hairy ape-like creatures are said to roam the deep forests of which region of the United States?
context: Sasquatch lore is concentrated in Washington, Oregon, and northern California. The name 'Bigfoot' was coined by a journalist after construction worker Jerry Crew found large prints in Humboldt County in 1958.

question: The Loch Ness Monster is supposed to live in a deep freshwater lake in which country?
context: Loch Ness is a 23-mile freshwater lake in the Scottish Highlands. The 'Surgeon's Photograph' from 1934 was the most famous image until a 1994 deathbed confession revealed it was a hoax using a toy submarine.

question: The Yeti, also called the Abominable Snowman, is said to inhabit which mountain range?
context: Sherpa folklore long predates Western reports. Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay reported strange large footprints on the 1953 Everest expedition, fueling Western Yeti enthusiasm for decades.

question: The Loch Ness Monster has a one-word nickname used affectionately around the world. What is it?
context: The nickname became standard in Scottish newspapers in the 1930s and now appears on everything from souvenir T-shirts to Inverness pub signs.

question: The Mothman is most associated with the small Ohio River town of Point Pleasant in which US state?
context: Sightings ran from November 1966 through December 15, 1967, when the Silver Bridge collapsed and killed 46 people. A 12-foot polished-steel statue of the creature stands in downtown Point Pleasant today.

question: The Jersey Devil is the legendary winged creature said to haunt the Pine Barrens of which state?
context: The Pine Barrens is a million-acre stretch of pinelands in southern New Jersey. The legend dates to the 18th century and the creature is said to be the cursed 13th child of one Mother Leeds.

question: The Bermuda Triangle is a stretch of which body of water famous for unexplained disappearances?
context: The triangle is roughly bounded by Miami, Bermuda, and Puerto Rico. The lore was popularized by a 1964 Argosy Magazine article. Statistical reviews find no higher disappearance rate than other busy ocean lanes.

question: The story of the lost continent of Atlantis was first told by which ancient Greek philosopher?
context: Atlantis appears in two of Plato's dialogues, Timaeus and Critias, around 360 BC. Most classicists read it as a moral parable invented by Plato; modern enthusiasts have nevertheless searched for it for centuries.

question: Stonehenge, the ring of standing stones built thousands of years ago, is located in which country?
context: Stonehenge stands on the Salisbury Plain in Wiltshire. The inner bluestones were quarried in the Preseli Hills of Wales and transported roughly 150 miles to the site.

question: When Governor John White returned to Roanoke Colony in 1590, what single word did he find carved on a tree where the settlers had been?
context: The Roanoke Colony was established in 1587 on the coast of present-day North Carolina. The 115 colonists vanished entirely before White's resupply ship returned. 'Croatoan' was the name of a nearby island and tribe.

question: The famous 1947 'flying disc' crash, debated as either a weather balloon or alien craft, happened near a town in which US state?
context: The crash site was near Roswell, New Mexico. The Army Air Forces initially reported recovering a 'flying disc,' then retracted to call it a weather balloon. A 1990s declassification revealed it was a Project Mogul nuclear-test-detection balloon.

question: Area 51, the famous classified Air Force facility surrounded by UFO lore, is located in the desert of which US state?
context: The base sits at Groom Lake, about 80 miles north of Las Vegas. The Air Force only officially acknowledged its existence in 2013, after decades of public records and even tour-bus jokes about it.

question: The Voynich Manuscript is famous because nobody has ever been able to do what to it?
context: The 240-page illustrated book dates to the 15th century. It contains an unknown script and drawings of plants nobody can identify. It now lives in Yale University's Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library.

question: The Yowie is a hairy ape-like cryptid from the folklore of indigenous people in which country?
context: Yowie traditions appear across many Aboriginal nations under different names. European settlers in the 19th century recorded their own 'hairy man' sightings, and modern Yowie hunters concentrate in eastern Australia.

question: The Great Pyramid of Giza, surrounded by countless 'who built it' theories, stands in which country?
context: The Great Pyramid was built around 2560 BC as a tomb for Pharaoh Khufu. Mainstream Egyptology attributes it to Egyptian laborers; alternative theories from Erich von Däniken to modern internet conspiracies persist.

question: The giant carved stone heads of Easter Island are called by what name?
context: Easter Island, called Rapa Nui by its people, lies in the South Pacific. The 887 monolithic moai were carved between roughly 1250 and 1500 AD. 2012 experimental archaeology showed they could be 'walked' upright with ropes.

question: The most famous Loch Ness Monster photo, taken in 1934, made Nessie a worldwide sensation. In 1994 it was revealed as a hoax — a toy submarine with a sculpted neck. What's the photo called?
context: Published April 21, 1934 by Dr. Robert Kenneth Wilson — a London gynaecologist — who claimed to have taken it while driving along the loch. The 'Surgeon' nickname came from his refusal to publicly attach his name. In 1994 Christian Spurling confessed on his deathbed that he, his stepfather Marmaduke Wetherell, and Wilson staged the photo with a toy submarine and a sculpted neck. Wetherell had been humiliated by the Daily Mail over a 'Nessie footprint' hoax and orchestrated the photo as revenge.

question: The skinwalker, a shape-shifting witch figure many people refuse to name out loud, comes from the tradition of which Native American people?
context: In Navajo language the figure is called yee naaldlooshii, 'by means of it, it goes on all fours.' Speaking the name is widely considered taboo. The modern 'Skinwalker Ranch' in Utah inherits the name without inheriting the religious context.

question: The wendigo, a starving cannibal spirit of the deep northern forests, comes from the folklore of which Native American people?
context: The wendigo legend belongs to Algonquian-speaking peoples across what is now Canada and the northern United States. The figure is associated with winter, famine, and the moral horror of cannibalism — never with hunger you can satisfy.

question: In Plato's story, Atlantis was destroyed when it sank beneath the waves of which body of water?
context: Plato placed Atlantis 'beyond the Pillars of Heracles,' i.e. beyond the Strait of Gibraltar in what we now call the Atlantic. The very name 'Atlantic' derives from the Greek 'sea of Atlas,' which the Atlantis story helped cement.

question: In 1971, an unknown man calling himself Dan Cooper hijacked a US passenger plane, was paid a $200,000 ransom, and then did what?
choices: Stowed away on the next flight
context: The hijacking happened on Thanksgiving Eve, November 24, 1971. He jumped from the rear airstair of a Northwest Orient Boeing 727 over southwestern Washington and was never identified. The press misheard 'Dan' as 'D.B.,' and the nickname stuck.

question: The Tunguska Event of 1908, a massive explosion that flattened 2,000 square kilometers of forest, happened in a remote part of which country?
context: The blast occurred above the Stony Tunguska River basin in Siberia on June 30, 1908. Most scientists attribute it to the airburst of a 50-meter meteoroid or comet fragment. No impact crater was ever found.

question: On the Something Awful forum in 2009, a Photoshop contest introduced a tall, suit-wearing, faceless figure stalking children. The character spawned games, comics, and a 2018 horror movie. What's it called?
context: Created by Eric Knudsen (handle 'Victor Surge') for a Something Awful Photoshop contest about supernatural images. Entrants were asked to alter photos to look like real paranormal documents. Slender Man's documents were photoshopped to look like archive shots of children with a faceless tall figure in the background. The character became a viral creepypasta, then the 2012 indie game Slender: The Eight Pages, then a 2018 movie. A tragic Wisconsin case in May 2014 brought the character to national news and a documentary, Beware the Slenderman.

question: The Chupacabra, said to drain blood from goats and other livestock, was first reported in 1995 on which Caribbean island?
context: The first sightings were near the town of Canóvanas, Puerto Rico. Witness Madelyne Tolentino later told folklorists she had recently seen the alien-creature film Species, whose monster strikingly resembles her chupacabra description.

question: The famous 1977 'Wow! Signal,' a strong narrow-band radio burst many think might be alien, was picked up by a telescope listening for what?
context: Astronomer Jerry Ehman, working on Ohio State's 'Big Ear' radio telescope SETI program, circled the printout in red pen and wrote 'Wow!' beside it. The 72-second signal has never been heard again.

question: December 1872, Atlantic: a ship is found drifting — sails set, cargo intact, lifeboat missing, and not a soul on board. Captain, wife, daughter, and seven crew all gone. What's the famous ghost ship?
context: The American brigantine Mary Celeste was found by the British ship Dei Gratia east of the Azores on December 4, 1872. Captain Briggs, his wife Sarah, daughter Sophia, and all seven crew were never seen again. The cargo of 1,701 alcohol barrels was intact; the lifeboat was missing. Modern theory: Briggs feared a hold-fire from leaking alcohol vapor and ordered evacuation; the ship sailed away from them. The archetypal ghost ship, referenced by Conan Doyle, Doctor Who, and countless others.

question: In 1958, construction worker Jerry Crew showed plaster casts of huge prints found at his Humboldt County, California logging site to a local newspaper. The reporter's article gave the unknown creature a memorable new English name. What was that name?
context: 'Sasquatch' was already in use, anglicized from the Halkomelem Salish word sasq'ets. 'Bigfoot' was the journalist's invention and quickly became the dominant North American name. The Crew casts are still on display in Willow Creek, California.

question: Roger Patterson and Bob Gimlin shot the most famous piece of Bigfoot footage ever recorded — a 53-second clip of a large dark figure striding across a sandbar at Bluff Creek in Northern California. In what year did they shoot it?
context: The film was shot on October 20, 1967. Patterson named the subject 'Patty.' Hollywood costume designers and biomechanics researchers have studied the gait, the muscle movement, and the unusual proportions of the figure for decades without consensus.

question: On December 15, 1967, the Silver Bridge between Point Pleasant, West Virginia and Gallipolis, Ohio collapsed during rush hour. Local lore tied the disaster to thirteen months of sightings of a winged red-eyed creature. How many people died in the bridge collapse?
context: The 1928 eyebar suspension bridge failed because of a cracked I-bar in a single eyebar; rush-hour cars and trucks plunged into the freezing Ohio River. John Keel's 1975 book The Mothman Prophecies tied the disaster to the cryptid sightings.

question: The 1934 'Surgeon's Photograph' of the Loch Ness Monster was attributed to a respected London medical man, which gave it credibility for decades. What was his profession?
context: Robert Kenneth Wilson said he had stopped to look at the loch on a road trip and snapped the photo. He kept his name out of newspaper credits for decades. The image was finally exposed as a hoax in a 1994 deathbed confession.

question: Sponge divers off a Greek island recovered a corroded bronze object from a 2,000-year-old shipwreck. X-rays later showed it was an intricate gear-driven calculator for tracking the sun, moon, and planets. What name was given to this device?
context: The divers found it in 1901 off the small island of Antikythera. The mechanism dates to around the 2nd century BC. Nothing of comparable complexity is known from antiquity, and nothing similar reappeared until medieval astronomical clocks more than a thousand years later.

question: The Voynich Manuscript, a 240-page illustrated 15th-century book written in an unknown script, is housed today in the rare-books library of which American university?
context: The manuscript lives in Yale's Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library. Polish-American antique dealer Wilfrid Voynich bought it in 1912. The script has resisted every cryptographic, linguistic, and AI-assisted attempt to decode it.

question: The Nazca Lines of Peru, including giant figures of a hummingbird, monkey, spider, and condor, share an unusual feature that makes them strange to anyone walking on the ground. What is it?
